extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians and scholars in history and philosophy of mathematics; informed mathematics community
extracted.subtask_description: A concise scholarly exposition of Bourbaki's notion of mathematical structure, its formal/metamathematical formulation (echelon constructions, species of structure), Bourbaki's stylistic and pedagogical practices, and the relation/tension between that structuralism and category theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical structure as set with relations/operations
rubrics_metrics.description: A mathematical structure is thought of as a set with relations and/or operations satisfying certain conditions (the contemporary informal characterization).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bourbaki's approach contains these elements but frames them within his own formalism: one works with underlying sets plus relations/operations placed on them. Example: a topology on A is realised as an OA in the echelon ℘(℘(A)) satisfying the usual open-set conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Echelon construction (construction of underlying sets)
rubrics_metrics.description: Underlying sets required for a species of structure must be constructed by an 'echelon construction' E: starting from basic sets A1,…,An and parameter sets B1,…,Bm, one closes under cartesian products and powersets in a specified recursive order to obtain the sets in E.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete requirement: if X and Y are in the echelon E then X×Y and ℘(X) must be in E; species of structure live on sets produced by such echelon constructions. This constrains what kinds of underlying sets/objects can be handled within Bourbaki's framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Species of structure defined by relations on an echelon
rubrics_metrics.description: A species of structure is defined by introducing relations R1,…,Rk and conditions on elements of a given echelon construction E.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The species is thus a pattern of relations placed on the particular echelon-constructed underlying sets. The presentation is metamathematical and given in formal set-theoretic language (Bourbaki even says a species of structure is a 'text').

rubrics_metrics.name: Transportability (isomorphism invariance)
rubrics_metrics.description: The relations defining a species of structure must be transportable: isomorphisms between lists of basic sets should yield 'the same' species of structures; theorems proven for one instance hold for any isomorphic instance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summarised by the phrase 'everything is done up to isomorphism'. This metamathematical constraint captures the essence of Bourbakian structuralism and is a central normative requirement for acceptable definitions of structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal/metamathematical framing of structures
rubrics_metrics.description: Bourbaki frames species of structure in a formal language for set theory and treats the notion metamathematically rather than by giving a single mathematical object-level definition of 'structure'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: Bourbaki's criteria are constraints on the formal apparatus and semantics within which theories are built (texts in the formal language), not a universal mathematical construction that covers all later notions like categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations: inability to treat categories as set-based species
rubrics_metrics.description: Categories in general cannot be reconstructed as Bourbakian species of structure because many important categories (e.g., Sets, Ab, R-Mod) cannot be represented as sets without restrictions—i.e., they lack suitable underlying sets for echelon constructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Options like moving to a theory of classes were available (Eilenberg & Mac Lane) but were not adopted; this limitation explains Bourbaki's failure to integrate category theory into his framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possible categories-first resolution requires morphisms/structural homomorphisms
rubrics_metrics.description: To subsume structures under categories one would need a notion of 'structural homomorphism' converting each type of structure into a category, thereby putting categories first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This approach requires every type of structure to come with an associated notion of morphism; historically some Bourbaki members (e.g., Weil) resisted this move as unjustified at the time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bourbaki's stylistic/pedagogical conventions for exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Bourbaki's written style is terse: definitions, theorems, proofs only; no discussion, no images, no context; many exercises viewed as integral; proofs not written fully in a formal system but assumed translatable by a competent reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical consequences: the exposition presupposes 'mathematical maturity' and is organized as an axiomatic development—material is developed from a few well-chosen axioms and by purely logical means. This is a prescriptive model for how to present mathematics in the Bourbakian mode.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapting structuralism to new foundations (requirement of transportability in new frameworks)
rubrics_metrics.description: To accommodate categories (and higher categories) within a structuralist viewpoint one must rethink foundations and build in the requirement that relations defining structures be transportable with respect to an appropriate notion of isomorphism in the new formal/semantic framework.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Candidates for such foundational frameworks include homotopy type theory and Makkai's FOLDS. The key normative point inherited from Bourbaki is the metamathematical constraint of transportability rather than a unique object-level definition of structure.
